x: The board this site started with. You list your own X profile, pick an amount, and the ten highest sit on the page in the order the money puts them. No follower count is consulted and no algorithm is asked. It is the one ranking on X that anybody can enter and everybody can read.
instagram: Instagram decides who is seen by a system nobody outside the company can inspect. This board decides it with a number anyone can check. List your own handle, pay more than the profile above you, and you pass it the moment the payment clears. Ten places, and the tenth is $2 away from being taken back.
tiktok: A TikTok account is buried or promoted by a recommendation engine that changes without notice. Here the order is a column of figures. You list yourself, you can see exactly what first place costs, and the only way past someone is to pay more than they did. Ten places, held for thirty days from the last payment.
youtube: Ten YouTube channels, ordered by what their owners paid to stand there. Subscriber counts are somebody else's measurement of you; this is your own. List your channel, choose a figure, and the board rearranges itself around it. Nothing here is editorial and nothing is recommended -- the money is the whole ranking.
facebook: Pages on Facebook reach whoever the feed decides that week. A place on this board reaches whoever opens the page, in the order money puts them. List your own page, pay above the one in front of you, and take its place. The ten are public and so is the price of passing each of them.
telegram: Telegram channels have no public league table -- growth happens in private and stays there. This is the visible version: ten channels, ranked by what their owners were willing to pay to be seen first. List your own, and the figure you pay is both your rank and the price somebody else has to beat.
snapchat: Snapchat keeps its numbers to itself, which leaves nothing for anyone to point at. Ten places here, in the order of what was paid for them, and the whole ledger is on the page. List your own profile from $2 and the board sorts itself. There is no application and nobody approves you.
twitch: Streamers are ranked everywhere by concurrent viewers, which rewards whoever streams the longest. This board is ranked by money, which rewards whoever wants it most. You list your own channel and the ten sort themselves by the figures. First place is always for sale, and its price is printed on the page.
linkedin: A LinkedIn profile gets seen by whoever the network decides to show it to. Here you decide, by paying more than the profile above yours. Ten places, one column of numbers, no endorsements and no connections required. It is the plainest possible statement of position: what you paid, and who paid more.
threads: Threads is young enough that nobody has a public standing on it yet. This board is one: ten profiles, ordered by what their owners paid. List your own, and every figure on the page is the exact amount somebody has to beat to get past you. Thirty days from the last payment, and the row is yours.
playstation: Ten PlayStation gamertags, ordered by money rather than trophies. Trophy level says how much you have played; this says how much you wanted the top row. You list your own PSN ID, and passing the tag above you costs exactly one dollar more than they have paid in total.
xbox: An Xbox gamerscore is earned over years and cannot be bought. A place on this board can be, which is the point: it is a different question with a different answer. List your own gamertag, put an amount against it, and the ten arrange themselves. Nothing about your play affects the order.
nintendo: Friend codes are how Nintendo players find each other and are almost impossible to publish anywhere useful. Here ten of them sit on one page, ordered by what their owners paid to be at the top. List your own, and the code stays on the board for thirty days after your last payment.
games: Which game belongs at number one is an argument with no referee. This board gives it one that cannot be disputed: money. Anybody can put a game up -- their own, or the one they will defend -- and the ten reorder as payments land. The cover art comes from the publisher's own store listing.
nba-teams: Thirty franchises, ten places, and no season required. A fan pays to push their club up and the standing changes that minute -- which is the opposite of how basketball works and exactly why the argument is fun. The list is closed to the thirty real teams; anything else typed here is a mistake worth refusing.
nba-players: Fifty of the league's leading scorers are offered as a starting list, taken from the NBA's own numbers rather than from memory. You are not listing yourself: you are backing somebody. Whoever their supporters pay the most for stands first, and the order changes with every payment rather than with every game.
nhl-teams: Thirty-two clubs and ten places on the page. Standings are decided in eighty-two games; this is decided by whoever cares enough to pay for the row. The list is closed -- a league has thirty-two teams and never a thirty-third -- so the only thing in question is the order.
nhl-players: Fifty skaters, ranked here by their supporters rather than by points. The suggestion list comes from the NHL's own season totals and is rebuilt rather than typed, so it is right after a trade. Back whoever you think belongs first; the person on the board is not the person paying.
football-clubs: Thirty clubs are offered and any club can be typed. What settles the order is money paid by supporters, not trophies, revenue or coefficient -- a table that no federation publishes and no ranking system produces. Ten places, and the price of first is whatever the current holder has paid, plus a dollar.
football-players: Every generation argues about who the best is and every argument ends the same way, with nothing settled. This one ends with a number. Back a player, and the ten sort by what was paid for each. The player has nothing to do with it and receives nothing -- this is a ranking on this website.
f1-drivers: Twenty drivers on the grid and one championship table that takes a season to write. This one is rewritten the moment somebody pays. Back the driver you would defend in an argument, and the ten reorder around the figures. The drivers are not involved and are not paid.
golf-players: Fifty golfers, offered as a list and open to any name. The official world ranking is a two-year rolling average of results; this is the other kind of ranking, the one made of how strongly people feel. Ten places, ordered by money paid, and the order changes the second it does.
ufc-fighters: Thirty fighters on the UFC's current rosters, and the pound-for-pound argument that never ends. Here it ends the way arguments end when somebody puts money on it. Back a fighter and the ten reorder; the fighters take no part and are paid nothing. The mark is drawn, not borrowed -- a promotion's logo is its own.
mma-fighters: Mixed martial arts is older and wider than any one promotion, so this board is not a company's roster: Fedor never signed with the UFC and a list without him would be a list about contracts. Thirty names to start from, any name accepted, and the order settled by what supporters paid.
boxers: Four sanctioning bodies, four champions per division, and no agreement anywhere on who is actually first. Boxing has always settled that at the gate. This board does the same thing in public: thirty names offered, any name accepted, and the ten ordered by the money put behind them.
bellator: Bellator built a roster deep enough to argue about on its own terms, and a fighter who tops it is topping something real. Thirty names, ranked here by what supporters paid rather than by a promotion's own ranking. The fighters are not involved; this is a leaderboard on this website and nothing more.
one-championship: ONE runs Muay Thai, kickboxing, submission grappling and mixed rules under one banner, which makes any single ranking of its fighters an argument by construction. This board settles it with money instead of a committee. Thirty names to start, any name allowed, and ten places that change as payments land.
pfl: A season, a bracket and a million-dollar final make the PFL the one promotion with a ranking built into its format. This is the other ranking: who supporters would put money behind, in public, before the season decides anything. Ten places, ordered by what was paid.
crypto: A thousand coins are offered here and the market ranks them by capitalisation every second of every day. This board ranks them by conviction: what people were willing to pay to put a coin at the top. The two orders disagree, and that disagreement is the only interesting thing about either of them.
memecoins: Memecoins are worth exactly what attention makes them worth, which makes a board of them unusually honest -- attention is the asset and this is a page that measures it in dollars. Ten coins, ordered by money paid, logos from CoinGecko. Nothing here is advice and nothing here is a price prediction.
exchanges: Every exchange claims to be the biggest by a volume figure it reports itself. This board reports something that cannot be inflated: what somebody actually paid to put a name in first place. Ten exchanges, one public ledger, and no listing fee that anybody has to be told about privately.
gifts: Airdrops and giveaways are announced everywhere and drown in the noise the same day. A place here is a place on a page that stays: ten projects, ordered by money, held for thirty days after the last payment. List your own giveaway from $2 and the board sorts itself around it.
artists: Streaming counts measure listening; charts measure sales. Neither measures the thing people actually argue about, which is who matters most. This board asks that question and takes payment as the answer. Ten artists, any name accepted, and the money is public down to the cent.
movies: Box office decides one ranking of films and critics decide another, and neither settles anything at a table with friends. This one is settled the moment someone pays. Put up the film you would defend, and the ten sort themselves by what was paid. Nothing is scored, reviewed or recommended here.
actors: An actor's standing is measured by awards, by box office, and by opinion, in that order of formality and reverse order of honesty. Here it is measured by money put down in public. Ten places, any name, and the figures on the page are the whole ranking.
podcasts: Podcast charts are built from downloads that the platforms do not publish and cannot be checked. This board is built from payments that are printed on the page to the cent. List your own show or back somebody else's; ten places, thirty days, and the price of first place is always visible.
cars: Marques argue about heritage, top speed and quarter-mile times, and every measure has a manufacturer behind it. This one has nobody behind it: ten marques, ordered by what enthusiasts paid to put each one first. It settles nothing about engineering and everything about who cares more.
boats: Yacht builders are ranked by length, by launches and by the size of the last hull delivered. None of those is the argument owners actually have. This board takes payments instead: ten builders, in the order people put money behind them, and the whole ledger on the page.
cities: Liveability indexes rank cities on criteria their authors chose. This one has one criterion, stated openly: what people paid to put their city first. Any city can be typed and ten hold the page. It is a measure of attachment, not of infrastructure, and it does not pretend otherwise.
pets: A pet with ten thousand followers and a pet with none are the same pet to everyone who knows them. This is a board for saying so in public: list your own animal, pay what you like, and the ten sort themselves. It costs $2 to be first and nothing to look.
restaurants: Guides send inspectors and review sites average out strangers. Neither is a ranking a restaurant can enter on its own terms. This one is: list your own place, pay what a position is worth to you, and the ten sit on a public page with the figures beside them.
startups: Funding rounds are a ranking of who convinced investors; this is a ranking of who convinced themselves. Thirty companies are offered as a starting list and any name is accepted. Ten places, ordered by money paid, and the amount is on the page rather than in a press release.
us-parties: Thirty American parties are offered, from the two everybody names to the ones that appear on a single state's ballot. The board settles which of them somebody will pay to see first -- a question no primary asks and no poll measures. A place here is paid advertising on a private website. It is not a poll, not an election, not a donation, and it is not counted anywhere but on this page.
us-politicians: Every sitting member of Congress, plus the presidents and vice presidents, all 566 names, kept current from the public-domain congressional dataset and shown with their official portraits. Anyone can be backed and the ten sort by what supporters paid. A place here is paid advertising on a private website. It is not a poll, not an election, not a donation, and it is not counted anywhere but on this page.
eu-parties: The European parties and the groups they actually sit in -- EPP, S&D, Renew, ECR, Patriots for Europe, Greens/EFA, The Left, ESN -- twenty-one names in all. Which of them somebody will pay to put first is a question the Parliament's own arithmetic never asks. A place here is paid advertising on a private website. It is not a poll, not an election, not a donation, and it is not counted anywhere but on this page.
eu-politicians: All 719 sitting Members of the European Parliament, from the Parliament's own list, each with their country and political group, and 710 of them with the official portrait. Back whoever you would defend; the ten sort by what was paid. A place here is paid advertising on a private website. It is not a poll, not an election, not a donation, and it is not counted anywhere but on this page.
movements: Fifteen American movements, from abolition and suffrage to the ones being argued about this week. They belong to nobody, which is why they are here rather than under a country's flag, and why the order is decided by money instead of by membership. A place here is paid advertising on a private website. It is not a poll, not an election, not a donation, and it is not counted anywhere but on this page.
x-influencers: Not your own profile -- somebody else's. Who the biggest creator on X is gets argued for free every day and never settled; this board settles it with a figure. Thirty handles offered, any handle accepted, and the ten reorder as supporters pay. The creators take no part and receive nothing.
instagram-influencers: Follower counts rank Instagram creators and everybody knows how little that measures. Here the ranking is what their audiences will actually pay to put them first, which is a smaller number and a truer one. Thirty handles to start from, ten places, and every figure public.
tiktok-influencers: TikTok makes and unmakes a creator's reach weekly, which means no ranking of them stays true for a month. This one changes the same way, but for a stated reason: somebody paid. Thirty handles offered, any handle accepted, and the ten sorted by money.
youtube-influencers: Subscriber counts on YouTube reward whoever started earliest. This board rewards whoever has the audience that will act today. Thirty channels offered and any channel accepted; the ten sort by what supporters paid, and the creators are not involved in it.
facebook-influencers: Facebook's biggest pages are largely invisible outside their own feeds, and there is no public league table of the people behind them. This is one: thirty handles to start, any handle accepted, ten places ordered by money paid, and nothing about it depends on Facebook's numbers.
us-billionaires: Nine hundred Americans are billionaires and thirty of them are offered here, from Musk and Bezos down. Forbes ranks them by what they own. This board ranks them by what other people will pay to see them at the top, which is a different question and gets a different answer. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
uk-billionaires: Fifty-two British billionaires, and the ones at the top are not the names a stranger would guess -- hedge fund managers and chemical fortunes rather than the household brands. Thirty are offered here and the ten are ordered by money paid, not by net worth. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
switzerland-billionaires: Forty-one Swiss billionaires for nine million people, which is the highest concentration in Europe and mostly invisible: shipping, medical devices, private equity, chemicals. Thirty are offered here, and the ten on the page are whoever people paid to put there. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
uae-billionaires: Eight Emiratis are billionaires, which would make a thin board -- so this one takes the country's residents as well, the people who actually live in Dubai and Abu Dhabi and mostly hold another passport. That is the UAE rich list as anybody outside the country would recognise it. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
japan-billionaires: Thirty-one Japanese billionaires, built on retail, sensors, video games and property rather than on the conglomerates the country is known for abroad. Thirty are offered here and the order on the page is decided by payments, not by portfolios. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
australia-billionaires: Australian fortunes are mining and software in almost equal measure -- iron ore on one side, Atlassian and Canva on the other -- which makes this a board with two entirely separate arguments on it. Fifty-one qualify and thirty are offered. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
china-billionaires: Four hundred and thirty-two Chinese billionaires, the second largest group in the world, and the names change faster than any other country's. Thirty are offered here: batteries, e-commerce, beverages, semiconductors, and the founder of TikTok at the top. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
israel-billionaires: Forty Israeli billionaires for nine million people, and the sources read like a map of the economy: shipping, defence, gambling software, and an unusual number of security startups sold in the last five years. india-billionaires: Two hundred and ten Indian billionaires and the two at the top -- Ambani and Adani -- are argued about more than anybody else on this list. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. germany-billionaires: One hundred and eighty-one German billionaires, and almost none of them are famous: discount supermarkets, fasteners, auto parts, pharmaceuticals, held by families that never gave an interview. Thirty are offered here, and the ten are ordered by what somebody paid. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
france-billionaires: Fifty French billionaires, and the top of the list is luxury -- LVMH, Chanel, L'Oreal, Kering -- which is unusual: almost nowhere else does fashion out-earn technology. Thirty are offered here and the ten are ordered by payments. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
canada-billionaires: Seventy-seven Canadian billionaires, with an unusual number made in crypto and software rather than in resources. Thirty are offered here. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. italy-billionaires: Seventy-five Italian billionaires: Nutella, eyeglass frames, luxury fashion, cement and, at the very top, two men from a cryptocurrency company. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. brazil-billionaires: Fifty-nine Brazilian billionaires -- beer, banking, beef and media, plus the co-founder of Facebook who lives in Singapore and still counts as Brazilian. The suggestion list is the country's billionaires as Forbes counts them, richest first, rebuilt from their live feed rather than typed from memory. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
russia-billionaires: One hundred and twenty-seven Russian billionaires, almost all of them built on metals, oil, gas and fertiliser, and most of them sanctioned somewhere. Thirty are offered here. This board takes no view on any of that: it records what people paid, and nothing else. Backing somebody here ranks them on this website and nothing else; they take no part in it and receive nothing.
saudi-arabia-billionaires: Eleven Saudi billionaires are counted publicly, which is fewer than the country's size suggests -- most Saudi wealth is not held in a form anybody publishes. south-korea-billionaires: Forty South Korean billionaires and the top of the list is one family -- four Samsung heirs in the first four places.
